newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland must join EMU if meets criteria -professor.
newsitem.headline: Finland must join EMU if meets criteria -professor.

text.p: Finland is obliged to join the third stage of European economic and monetary union if it meets the entry criteria, but would be unlikely to be forced into EMU against its will, a legal expert said on Tuesday.

The Finnish parliament's coming vote on EMU-membership will be only a political gesture, but important in the sense that it will be binding for the prime minister at the spring 1998 EU summit, Martin Scheinin, associate professor of constitutional law at the University of Helsinki, wrote in a new book.
"Participation in...the single currency is a treaty obligation...if Finland meets with the conditions...," he said.

"The treaty obligations related to stage three (of EMU) have already been approved and incorporated by the parliament," Scheinin said, referring to the legislature's November 1994 vote by a two thirds majority in favour of Finnish membership of the European Union.
"The decision still to be made by the parliament on Finland's participation in stage three will be of a political nature," he said, adding "a simple majority decision is sufficient".
He ruled out the possibility that parliament would have to vote for EMU by a two thirds majority to approve membership.

The prime minister, not the president, should represent Finland at the summit of EU heads of state and government -- scheduled for spring 1998 -- at which the founding members of the single currency will be chosen, Scheinin said.
"Finland will be represented by the prime minister, not the president," he said, noting the latter had participated in EU meetings related to foreign and security policy.

As the prime minister is accountable to parliament, "a political decision by the Finnish parliament on Finland's will to participate in the single currency right from the beginning of stage three will be binding in relation to the conduct of the prime minister in the meeting of the council," Scheinin said.

The decisions on which countries can join EMU will be made by the European Council by qualified majority and so "it is politically unlikely but juridically possible that a state meeting the conditions of participating in the single currency would be required to do so against its own will," he said.
